hypothesis: If Darwin's claim holds, no native, non-volant, non-marine mammal species is restricted to islands lying more than about 300 miles (about 483 km) from a continent or large continental island.
pass_criterion: Take the Mammal Diversity Database (MDD) v2.5 rows that are wild, extant or recently extinct, not in Chiroptera, and not marine (exclude Cetacea, Sirenia, pinnipeds, Enhydra lutris, Lontra felina, Ursus maritimus). Keep species whose countryDistribution lists only oceanic-island countries or territories: Cabo Verde, Mauritius, Seychelles, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Nauru, Palau, Micronesia, Marshall Islands, Cook Islands, Solomon Islands, New Zealand and Iceland. Remove species recorded as introduced. Then check each remaining island against an external distance measure (great-circle distance to the nearest continental coast or large continental island such as Greenland, New Guinea, Madagascar, Borneo or Great Britain). The claim passes if, after manual adjudication, the count of native non-volant terrestrial species endemic to islands more than 483 km from such a landmass is 0.
fail_criterion: The claim fails if at least 1 native non-volant terrestrial mammal species (extant or recently extinct) occurs only on islands more than 483 km from a continent or large continental island, and its nativeness is not disputed in the MDD taxonomyNotes field or the cited authority. Darwin said "free from doubt", so one clear case refutes it. The endemic rodents of the Solomon Islands are the main expected test case. If every candidate is either nearer than 483 km or is a recorded introduction, the claim is not refuted.
interpretation: "Terrestrial mammal" is read as any non-volant, non-marine wild mammal. Bats are excluded, as Darwin excluded them in the same chapter. "Domesticated animals kept by the natives" corresponds to the MDD domestic flag and to introduced species, which are excluded. "Island above 300 miles from a continent or great continental island" is read as 483 km great-circle distance to the nearest continental coast or large continental-shelf island. MDD does not record distances, so a country-level proxy is used: the candidate island nations are listed in the pass criterion, and their distances come from standard geography outside the dataset. Recently extinct species are counted because Darwin's rule concerns native fauna, not only survivors. The unit is a species under modern taxonomy, which splits many forms Darwin treated as one. Islands on a continental shelf, joined to the mainland in the Pleistocene, count as continental; deep-water islands such as the Solomons, beyond the Sahul shelf, count as oceanic.

dataset.name: Mammal Diversity Database (Version v2.5, published July 28, 2026)
dataset.publisher: Mammal Diversity Database, American Society of Mammalogists (via Zenodo)
dataset.why_it_fits: The page lists a downloadable CSV, MDD_v2.5_6904species.csv, with one row per accepted mammal species. Fields to use: order, family, genus, specificEpithet, countryDistribution, subregionDistribution, continentDistribution, biogeographicRealm, taxonomyNotes, and the extinct and domestic flags. These allow filtering to non-bat, non-marine, wild species restricted to named oceanic-island countries. The exact column names for the extinct and domestic flags must be read from the CSV header or META_v2.5.csv.
